records.title: Birth at Mhow — 14 April 1891
records.location: Mhow, Central Provinces (now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, Madhya Pradesh)
records.description: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born on 14 April 1891 at Mhow, a military cantonment town where his father Ramji Maloji Sakpal served as a Subedar in the British Indian Army. His mother was Bhimabai Sakpal. He was the fourteenth and last child of the family.
records.significance: The birthplace is today marked by the Bhim Janmabhoomi memorial and is the starting point of the early-life gallery timeline.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1 (Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment); Dr. Ambedkar Foundation biographical record.

media.label: Birth record summary
media.note: Text summary authored for this platform.

media.label: Visualisation: cantonment street, Mhow, 1890s
media.note: Procedurally generated reconstruction. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: The Sakpal family and cantonment life
records.description: Ramji Sakpal, a Subedar in the army, valued education and moved the family with his postings. After his retirement the family settled in Satara district and then in Bombay. The household language at home was Marathi, with English schooling from an early age.
records.significance: The family's emphasis on schooling is one of the reasons Ambedkar's education could continue at all, despite the social exclusion the family faced.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1; standard biographical record.

records.title: Schooling at Satara — Elphinstone Road High School
records.description: Ambedkar attended government high school at Satara. Accounts recorded in his own writings and in the standard biographies describe the social exclusion he met there, including being made to sit apart from other pupils and being denied access to the common drinking water.
records.significance: These experiences form the documentary basis of the early-life gallery's section on exclusion and the determination to study — the phrase 'Educate, Agitate, Organise' is closely associated with the movement he later led.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1 (autobiographical notes and letters); standard biographical record.

media.label: School-record reconstruction
media.note: Facsimile-style reconstruction prepared for exhibition. It is not an original document.

records.title: Matriculation — 1908
records.description: Ambedkar passed the matriculation examination of the University of Bombay in 1908, studying at Elphinstone High School. Contemporary records note that he was the first student from the community to reach this stage in the region.
records.significance: Matriculation opened the route to college and became a landmark in the archive timeline of Indian educational history.
records.source: University of Bombay records as cited in standard biographical accounts; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1.

records.title: Marriage to Ramabai — 1906
records.description: In 1906, at about the age of fifteen, Ambedkar was married to Ramabai, in keeping with the customs of the time. Ramabai took part in the Mahad satyagraha of 1927 and stood with him through the years of study and political work. She died on 27 May 1935.
records.significance: Her participation at Mahad is documented in accounts of the satyagraha and is presented in both the Early Life and Social Reform galleries.
records.source: Standard biographical record; accounts of the Mahad satyagraha (1927); Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

media.label: Biographical note
media.note: Authored summary, no photograph available in the archive for this record.

records.title: Elphinstone College, Bombay — B.A. 1912
records.description: Ambedkar studied Political Science and Economics at Elphinstone College, Bombay, graduating with the degree of Bachelor of Arts in 1912. His performance brought him to the notice of patrons who supported his further study abroad.
records.significance: This is the academic bridge from Satara to Columbia University and the London School of Economics.
records.source: University of Bombay / Elphinstone College record as cited in standard biographical accounts.

records.title: The Gaekwad scholarship — 1913
records.description: Sayajirao Gaekwad III, Maharaja of Baroda, supported Ambedkar's higher education abroad through a scholarship, on terms that included entering the service of Baroda State after his studies.
records.significance: State patronage at this point made the Columbia and London years possible. The scholarship arrangement is a documented example of early institutional support for education of the community.
records.source: Baroda State records as cited in standard biographical accounts; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1.

media.label: Scholarship undertaking (reconstruction)
media.note: Facsimile-style reconstruction, not the original instrument.

records.title: Columbia University, New York — 1913–1916
records.location: Columbia University, New York, United States
records.description: Ambedkar joined Columbia University in 1913, studying economics, sociology and anthropology. He was awarded the degree of Master of Arts in 1915. Among his teachers was the philosopher and educationist John Dewey, whose ideas on democracy and education are frequently cited in studies of Ambedkar's later writing. His paper 'Castes in India' was presented at an anthropology seminar at Columbia in May 1916.
records.significance: The Columbia years produced the first scholarly formulation of his analysis of caste, and connect the Indian social reform movement to a wider international intellectual context.
records.source: Columbia University Libraries, Rare Book & Manuscript Library — B. R. Ambedkar collection and university record.

media.label: Visualisation: Columbia seminar room, 1916
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: “Castes in India: Their Mechanism, Genesis and Development” — 1916
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A paper prepared for an anthropology seminar at Columbia University and delivered on 9 May 1916. It examines caste as a system, arguing that endogamy is its central mechanism, and was published in the Indian Antiquary in 1917.
records.significance: The earliest sustained piece of Ambedkar's scholarly writing on caste, written two decades before 'Annihilation of Caste'.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1 (Government of Maharashtra / Dr. Ambedkar Foundation).

media.label: Paper text viewer
media.note: Full text to be attached from a public-domain edition by the content team.

records.title: London School of Economics and Gray's Inn — 1916–1923
records.location: London School of Economics; Gray's Inn, London
records.description: Ambedkar studied at the London School of Economics, where he was awarded the degree of Master of Science in Economics in 1921 and later the degree of Doctor of Science in Economics in 1923. He was called to the Bar at Gray's Inn in 1923. His studies were interrupted and resumed more than once for want of funds.
records.significance: These years gave the legal and economic grounding that later shaped his work on the Constitution and on public finance.
records.source: LSE Library archives; Gray's Inn record as cited in standard biographical accounts.

media.label: Visualisation: LSE courtyard, 1920s
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: “The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution” — 1923
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A study of Indian currency and exchange policy, developed from his doctoral work in economics in London and published in 1923. It argues for a managed currency and a stable exchange standard for India.
records.significance: The most technical of his books; it belongs to the economic history collections of the archive and is the reason the Manuscript Gallery includes a currency-policy bay.
records.source: Original edition, P. S. King & Son, London, 1923 (public domain in many jurisdictions — verify locally).

media.label: Title page image
media.note: Reconstruction of a title page. Attach a genuine public-domain scan through the content-import system.

records.title: Professor of Political Economy, Sydenham College, Bombay — 1918–1920
records.location: Sydenham College of Commerce and Economics, Bombay
records.description: Between his two periods of study in London, Ambedkar taught at Sydenham College of Commerce and Economics in Bombay as Professor of Political Economy.
records.significance: Teaching in Bombay marks his return to Indian public life and precedes the founding of his newspapers and social organisations.
records.source: Standard biographical record; institutional history of Sydenham College, Bombay.

records.title: Doctorate in Economics, Columbia University — awarded 1927
records.description: Columbia University awarded Ambedkar the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in 1927 for a thesis titled 'The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India', which had been published in London in 1925 with a foreword by Edwin R. A. Seligman.
records.significance: The degree closes the 'student' arc of the early-life gallery and opens the public career that the remaining galleries cover.
records.source: Columbia University Libraries record; published edition, P. S. King & Son, London, 1925.

media.label: Thesis title page
media.note: Reconstruction; attach a genuine scan via content import.

records.title: Service in Baroda State
records.description: Ambedkar held appointment in Baroda State in 1913, and after returning from London in 1923 he again served briefly in Baroda before moving to Bombay. The period is recorded in his own recollections of difficulties encountered in securing accommodation and in office life.
records.significance: Documents the professional consequences of caste exclusion in employment and housing, a theme taken up in the Social Reform gallery.
records.source: Standard biographical record; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

records.title: “Mooknayak” — newspaper founded 1920
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (editor)
records.description: Mooknayak ('Leader of the Voiceless') was launched as a fortnightly in Marathi on 31 January 1920. It was among the first newspapers of the community in western India and received support from Shahu Chhatrapati of Kolhapur. It ceased publication within a few years.
records.significance: The beginning of Ambedkar's use of the printing press as a tool of social reform and mass education.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1; standard accounts of Marathi periodical history.

media.label: Visualisation: Marathi press room, 1920
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha — 1924
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (founder)
records.description: Founded in Bombay in 1924, the Sabha worked for the welfare of the 'excluded' (bahishkrit) communities, with programmes for education, hostels, and political representation. Ambedkar was the organising secretary.
records.significance: The first organisation founded by Ambedkar, and the institutional ancestor of the later political parties he led.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1 and Vol. 17; standard biographical accounts.

records.title: Mahad Satyagraha — 20 March 1927
records.location: Chavdar Lake (Chavdar Tale), Mahad, Raigad district, Maharashtra
records.description: A satyagraha asserting the right of the community to use the public water tank at Mahad. The Bombay government had earlier passed a resolution opening public places maintained out of public funds; the tank was used on 20 March 1927 with a large procession, and the action was repeated in December 1927.
records.significance: One of the defining actions of the movement for civic equality in the 1920s and the central event of the Social Reform gallery's interactive reconstruction.
records.source: Accounts of the Mahad satyagraha (1927); Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches; contemporary press record.

media.label: Visualisation: Mahad water tank, 1927
media.note: Procedurally generated reconstruction. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: Burning of the Manusmriti — 25 December 1927
records.description: At a conference held at Mahad in December 1927, a copy of the Manusmriti was publicly burnt as a symbolic protest against texts used to justify caste hierarchy.
records.significance: The event marks the movement's shift from petitioning for civic rights to a direct public repudiation of caste-ordering texts. The gallery presents it with the historical context of the debate about religious authority and social reform.
records.source: Accounts of the Mahad conference, December 1927; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

records.title: Kalaram Temple Satyagraha, Nashik — 1930–1935
records.description: A prolonged satyagraha for the right of entry into the Kalaram Temple at Nashik, led with the participation of volunteers from across the region. The temple remained closed to the community and the agitation was eventually discontinued.
records.significance: Together with Mahad, it is one of the two defining civil-rights campaigns of the 1927–1935 period, and it is often read as marking the point at which Ambedkar concluded that entry into existing religious institutions would not deliver equality.
records.source: Accounts of the Kalaram temple satyagraha; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

media.label: Visualisation: Nashik temple approach
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: Round Table Conferences, London — 1930–1932
records.description: Ambedkar attended the First and Second Round Table Conferences in London as a representative of the Depressed Classes, arguing for separate political representation. The Third Conference was not attended by the Indian National Congress.
records.significance: The constitutional-negotiation phase of the movement, and the immediate context of the Poona Pact of 1932.
records.source: Proceedings of the Round Table Conferences (1930–32), Government of India records.

media.label: Conference proceedings note
media.note: Authored summary; original proceedings to be attached via content import.

records.title: The Poona Pact — 24 September 1932
records.description: An agreement between Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi, negotiated while Gandhi was fasting at Yerwada Jail, which replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats within a joint electorate, together with provisions on representation in legislatures.
records.significance: One of the most consequential political settlements of the colonial period for the representation of the Depressed Classes. The gallery presents the competing arguments of both sides rather than a single verdict.
records.source: Text of the Poona Pact (1932), Government of India records; contemporary accounts.

media.label: Pact text (reconstruction layout)
media.note: Facsimile-style layout prepared for exhibition; attach the authentic text from a public record.

records.title: Independent Labour Party — founded 15 August 1936
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (founder)
records.description: A political party that contested elections under the Government of India Act of 1935, with a programme that addressed not only the Depressed Classes but also tenants and workers.
records.significance: Widened the movement's political base beyond a single community and delivered a block of seats in the 1937 elections.
records.source: Standard biographical and political history record; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

records.title: All India Scheduled Castes Federation — 1942
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (founder)
records.description: A political organisation formed in 1942 to press for the political and constitutional demands of the Scheduled Castes, particularly in the debates that preceded independence.
records.significance: Provides the organisational context for Ambedkar's entry into the Viceroy's Executive Council in 1942 and the Constituent Assembly in 1946.
records.source: Standard political history record; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

records.title: “Annihilation of Caste” — 1936
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: Written as a presidential address for the annual conference of the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal, a reformist body, to be held at Lahore in 1936. When the organisation asked him to revise the text, the address was not delivered; Ambedkar published it himself in the same year, together with a reply to Mahatma Gandhi's criticism of the text.
records.significance: The most widely read of his writings. It argues that caste cannot be removed by reforming customs alone, and that effective reform must address the authority that sustains caste. Presented in the gallery with a note that the published text and the Gandhi–Ambedkar exchange should be read together.
records.source: Original 1936 edition (public domain in many jurisdictions — verify locally); Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1.

media.label: Document reader with page-turn
media.note: Attach full public-domain text via content import.

records.title: “Bahishkrit Bharat” — newspaper founded 1927
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (editor)
records.description: A fortnightly newspaper begun in April 1927, in Marathi, which carried reports of the Mahad and Nashik campaigns and served to organise opinion between agitations. It was followed by the journal Janata in the late 1920s.
records.significance: The press as an instrument of mobilisation; the gallery's reading table reproduces its layout style as a labelled reconstruction.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches; standard accounts of Marathi periodical history.

records.title: Petitions and memoranda to the colonial government
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar and the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha
records.description: A body of written submissions made to commissions, conferences and the colonial administration between 1919 and 1932, arguing the case for education, representation and civil rights for the Depressed Classes.
records.significance: Shows the constitutional-petition phase of the movement and the documentary method that later appears in 'States and Minorities' (1947).
records.source: Colonial-era government records as compiled in Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

records.title: The Constituent Assembly of India
records.location: New Delhi (Constitution Hall, later the Central Hall of Parliament)
records.description: The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 to frame a constitution for India. Ambedkar was elected to it from the Bombay constituency in July 1946, having earlier served as a member of the Viceroy's Executive Council from 1942.
records.significance: The chamber in which the archive's constitutional content originates; the Constitutional Gallery simulates its seating plan as an unlabelled-anonymous digital reconstruction.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates (Government of India, public record).

media.label: Visualisation: Assembly chamber layout
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: Chairman of the Drafting Committee — 29 August 1947
records.author: Constituent Assembly of India
records.description: On 29 August 1947 the Constituent Assembly appointed a Drafting Committee of seven members under the chairmanship of B. R. Ambedkar to prepare a draft constitution. Its members were Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, K. M. Munshi, Mohd. Saadulla, B. L. Mitter and D. P. Khaitan. The Committee worked from the reports of the Union Powers Committee, the Union Constitution Committee and the Provincial Constitution Committee.
records.significance: The formal origin of the document that the Constitutional Gallery displays; the exhibit states the Committee's composition so that the work is not attributed to one person alone.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. V (29 August 1947); Government of India records.

media.label: Visualisation: drafting table, 1947
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

media.label: Draft Constitution structure viewer
media.note: Structural summary; attach the authentic text from a public record.

records.title: The Objectives Resolution — 13 December 1946
records.author: Jawaharlal Nehru (moved)
records.description: The resolution that set out the guiding aims of the constitution — sovereignty of the people, justice, liberty, equality and the safeguarding of the interests of minorities — was moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. Its phrasing underlies the Preamble of the Constitution.
records.significance: Explains why the Preamble reads as it does; the gallery links the Resolution text to the Preamble text in a side-by-side comparison.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. I (13 December 1946 and 22 January 1947).

media.label: Resolution text panel
media.note: Text to be attached from Constituent Assembly Debates, a public record.

records.title: The Preamble — “We, the People of India”
records.author: Constituent Assembly of India
records.description: The Preamble declares the source of the Constitution's authority to be the people of India, and sets out its objects: justice — social, economic and political; liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; equality of status and of opportunity; and fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation.
records.significance: The interpretive key to the whole Constitution and the first exhibit of the Constitutional Gallery.
records.source: Constitution of India, Preamble (Government of India; text available through India Code).

media.label: Preamble text panel
media.note: Attach the authentic text from India Code.

records.title: Fundamental Rights — Part III, Articles 12 to 35
records.author: Constituent Assembly of India
records.description: Part III of the Constitution guarantees fundamental rights, including equality before the law (Article 14), prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15), equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16), abolition of untouchability (Article 17), freedom of speech and expression (Article 19), protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21), freedom of religion (Articles 25 to 28), and the right to constitutional remedies (Article 32).
records.significance: The constitutional core of the equality agenda documented in the earlier galleries. Article 17 in particular responds directly to the social practices examined in the Social Reform gallery.
records.source: Constitution of India, Part III (Government of India; text available through India Code).

media.label: Article browser
media.note: Article summaries authored for this platform; attach authoritative text.

records.title: Article 32 — “the very soul ... and the very heart of it”
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: Speaking in the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, Ambedkar described Article 32 — the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights — as the provision that makes the rights effective, calling it the very soul and the very heart of the Constitution.
records.significance: A documented instance of his approach to constitutional design: a right without a remedy is not a right. The gallery presents it as a quoted extract with a full citation to the Debates.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. XI, 25 November 1949 (Government of India, public record).

media.label: Reading of the extract (platform voice)
media.note: This is a modern narration reading, not a recording of the original speech.

records.title: “Constitutional morality” — Constituent Assembly, 4 November 1948
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: In the debate on the draft constitution Ambedkar argued that constitutional forms would not by themselves sustain a democracy, and spoke of the need for a constitutional morality — a habit of respecting the means and methods of constitutional government — in addition to the letter of the document.
records.significance: The gallery's 'constitutional morality' interactive exhibit, and one of the concepts most frequently cited in civic-education material.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. VII, 4 November 1948 (Government of India, public record).

records.title: “Political democracy cannot last unless … social democracy” — 25 November 1949
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: In his concluding address on the adoption of the Constitution, Ambedkar argued that political democracy rests on a social foundation, and that a society built on inequality of status cannot sustain democratic institutions merely by holding elections.
records.significance: Links the constitutional gallery back to the social reform gallery; used as the closing note of the final knowledge challenge.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. XI, 25 November 1949 (Government of India, public record).

media.label: Reading of the extract (platform voice)
media.note: Modern narration; not an original recording.

records.title: Directive Principles of State Policy — Part IV
records.author: Constituent Assembly of India
records.description: Part IV sets out the principles that guide the State in making policy, including the promotion of the welfare of the people, the reduction of inequalities in income and status (Article 38), and the promotion of the educational and economic interests of the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections, with protection from social injustice and exploitation (Article 46).
records.significance: Article 46 is the constitutional instruction that corresponds to the education mission at the centre of this archive.
records.source: Constitution of India, Part IV (Government of India; text available through India Code).

records.title: “States and Minorities” — memorandum, 1947
records.location: Submitted to the Constituent Assembly of India
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A memorandum submitted on behalf of the All India Scheduled Castes Federation proposing constitutional safeguards for the Depressed Classes, including provisions on fundamental rights, representation and the settlement of villages.
records.significance: The bridge between the Social Reform gallery's campaigns and the constitutional text exhibited in the Constitutional Gallery.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 1.

records.title: Adoption of the Constitution — 26 November 1949
records.author: Constituent Assembly of India
records.description: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution of India on 26 November 1949. The document came into force on 26 January 1950, the date now observed as Republic Day. Since 2015, 26 November is observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).
records.significance: The central date of the Constitutional Gallery's timeline, and the anchor for the platform's constitutional-education content.
records.source: Constituent Assembly Debates, Vol. XI; Government of India notifications on Constitution Day.

media.label: Visualisation: Assembly adopts the Constitution
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: The Constitution comes into force — 26 January 1950
records.author: Government of India
records.description: On 26 January 1950 the Constitution of India came into force, India became a republic, and the Constituent Assembly became the Provisional Parliament. Dr. Rajendra Prasad took office as the first President of India.
records.significance: The moment the rights and institutions exhibited throughout the gallery acquired legal force.
records.source: Government of India records; Constitution of India, Article 394 (commencement).

records.title: First Law Minister of India — 1947 to 1951
records.description: Ambedkar served as the first Law Minister of independent India from 1947. He resigned from the Union Cabinet in 1951, after differences within the government over the Hindu Code Bill, which had been introduced to reform and codify Hindu personal law — including provisions affecting women's rights in marriage and inheritance.
records.significance: The resignation is presented alongside the substance of the Hindu Code Bill, because the bill and its fate are central to the record of his legislative work on gender and family law.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 14; parliamentary records of 1951.

records.title: The Hindu Code Bill — 1948 to 1951
records.author: Government of India
records.description: Introduced in 1948 and taken up again in the Provisional Parliament in 1951, the bill sought to codify and reform Hindu personal law, including monogamy, divorce, a daughter's share in inheritance, and adoption. It met substantial opposition, was divided into separate bills, and the reforms were enacted in stages between 1955 and 1956 — after Ambedkar had left the Cabinet.
records.significance: Presented in the gallery as an example of how constitutional principles of equality are carried into ordinary law, and how long that process can take.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 14; parliamentary records.

records.title: Member of the Rajya Sabha — 1952 to 1956
records.description: Ambedkar was elected to the Rajya Sabha in 1952 and remained a member of the Council of States until his death in December 1956, speaking on law, labour and social policy.
records.significance: Shows that his legislative work continued after 1951, outside the government.
records.source: Parliament of India records.

records.title: “Thoughts on Pakistan” — 1940
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: An examination of the demand for a separate state, later revised and republished as 'Pakistan or the Partition of India'. The book analyses the communal problem, the composition of Muslim society, and the political options open in the 1940s.
records.significance: Part of the archive's political-writing collection; the Manuscript Gallery presents it with a note on how the text relates to the partition debates of the period.
records.source: Original editions (1940, 1945/46) — verify public-domain status locally before displaying full text.

records.title: “Federation versus Freedom” — 1939
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A study of the federal provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, and their implications for representation — particularly for minorities — in a proposed Indian federation.
records.significance: Shows the constitutional-analytical work that precedes 1947, and is used in the gallery's 'before the drafting table' section.
records.source: Original edition (1939) — verify public-domain status locally.

records.title: “What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables” — 1945
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A detailed critique, with documentary appendices, of the Indian National Congress and of Gandhian approaches to the question of untouchability, written on the eve of independence.
records.significance: Presented as a primary source for the political disagreement between two leading figures of the period; the gallery pairs extracts with Gandhi's own positions so that visitors can read both.
records.source: Original 1945 edition — verify public-domain status locally; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

media.label: Paired-extracts reader
media.note: Editorial pairing prepared for exhibition, with citations.

records.title: “Who Were the Shudras?” — 1946
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A historical study of the formation of the four varnas, arguing that the Shudra category was produced through social and political conflict rather than being ordained from the beginning. It draws on textual and historical sources for its argument.
records.significance: A key example of Ambedkar as historian and textual critic rather than only as a political figure; shown with the note that its theses are debated by historians.
records.source: Original 1946 edition — verify public-domain status locally; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 7.

records.title: “The Untouchables: Who Were They and Why They Became Untouchables?” — 1948
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A companion volume to 'Who Were the Shudras?', in which Ambedkar sets out a theory of the origins of untouchability, drawing on evidence of the history of religious conflict, broken men and settlement patterns.
records.significance: Central to the gallery's section on the historical explanation of exclusion, presented with a clear statement that the theory is a scholarly argument, not settled historical consensus.
records.source: Original 1948 edition — verify public-domain status locally; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 7.

media.label: Theory summary with editorial note
media.note: Authored summary; flagged as a debated thesis.

records.title: “Riddles in Hinduism” — written in the 1950s, published posthumously
records.location: Written in Delhi · published by the Government of Maharashtra
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A set of critical essays on Hindu texts and traditions, written in the 1950s but left unpublished at his death; the work was published posthumously in 1987 in the Writings and Speeches series, and its publication was itself the subject of public debate.
records.significance: Included in the archive as an editorial case study: the gallery shows how questions of publication, consent and controversy attach to manuscripts after an author's death.
records.source: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 4 (Government of Maharashtra, 1987).

records.title: “The Buddha and His Dhamma” — completed 1956, published 1957
records.location: Bombay (published posthumously by the People's Education Society)
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: The last major work, written in the mid-1950s and published after his death in 1957. It presents the life and teachings of the Buddha together with Ambedkar's reading of Buddhism as a rational, socially engaged doctrine. He was working on the manuscript until shortly before his death.
records.significance: Directly connected to his conversion to Buddhism in October 1956; the Manuscript Gallery displays it last in the chronological bay.
records.source: First edition, People's Education Society, Bombay, 1957; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches, Vol. 11.

records.title: “Ranade, Gandhi and Jinnah” — 1943
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A lecture, published as a booklet, assessing three figures of Indian public life through the lens of political leadership and social reform.
records.significance: Part of the archive's collection of short political writings from the 1940s.
records.source: Original 1943 booklet — verify public-domain status locally.

records.title: “Mr. Gandhi and the Emancipation of the Untouchables” — 1943
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar
records.description: A short work setting out the differences between the positions of Gandhi and Ambedkar on the emancipation of the Depressed Classes, written while the second was serving on the Viceroy's Executive Council.
records.significance: Pairs with the paired-extracts reader in the Manuscript Gallery so that both positions can be examined from primary texts.
records.source: Original 1943 edition — verify public-domain status locally.

records.title: Chaitya Bhoomi — Dadar, Mumbai
records.description: The site at Dadar in Mumbai where Dr. Ambedkar was cremated on 7 December 1956, the day after his death. A memorial complex stands there today, and the site is the focus of the largest annual commemorations, particularly on 6 December and during Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din in October.
records.significance: The largest memorial site in the archive's map view; the gallery presents it as a place of remembrance and as an urban heritage site.
records.source: Dr. Ambedkar Foundation; standard biographical record of the cremation, December 1956.

records.title: Deekshabhoomi — Nagpur, Maharashtra
records.description: The site in Nagpur where, on 14 October 1956, Ambedkar embraced Buddhism together with a very large gathering of followers. A memorial stupa now stands on the site; it was completed and consecrated in 2001. The place is also the location of the annual Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din observances.
records.significance: The most architecturally distinctive memorial in the map view — a stupa dome — and the site that connects the Constitutional Gallery to the Legacy Archive.
records.source: Dr. Ambedkar Foundation; standard accounts of the conversion ceremony, October 1956.

records.title: Dr. Ambedkar National Memorial — 26 Alipur Road, Delhi
records.description: The house at 26 Alipur Road in Delhi is where Dr. Ambedkar lived during his last years and where he died on 6 December 1956. It was developed as a national memorial and inaugurated on 14 April 2018, managed under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
records.significance: The memorial most directly connected to the Ministry that owns this problem statement, and the setting for the archive's 'last years in Delhi' exhibit.

records.source: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation records on the National Memorial.

records.title: Rajgruha — the Dadar residence, Mumbai
records.description: The house in Hindu Colony, Dadar, built in the 1930s, where Ambedkar lived with his family and where his library was kept. The building holds a large collection of his books and is maintained as a memorial and museum.
records.significance: The gallery presents it as a scholar's working house, with a reconstruction of the library wall as the centrepiece of the memorial map.
records.source: Standard accounts of the Rajgruha memorial; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation.

records.title: Bhim Janmabhoomi — Mhow, Madhya Pradesh
records.description: The birthplace of Dr. Ambedkar at Mhow, now Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, marked by a memorial and a public library. It is a place of pilgrimage and a site of the annual birth-anniversary observances on 14 April.
records.significance: The earliest site in the memorial gallery, and the geographic starting point of the archive's map.
records.source: Dr. Ambedkar Foundation; Government of Madhya Pradesh records on the memorial.

records.title: Ambedkar Memorial Park — Gomti Nagar, Lucknow
records.description: A large memorial park in Gomti Nagar, Lucknow, dedicated to Dr. Ambedkar alongside other figures of social reform, laid out with sandstone colonnades, a central stupa and long reflecting water channels. It was inaugurated in 2008.
records.significance: The gallery's example of monumental public architecture dedicated to social-reform memory, and the largest reconstruction scene in the Memorial zone.
records.source: Government of Uttar Pradesh records on the Ambedkar Memorial Park.

records.title: Statue of Dr. Ambedkar — Hyderabad, Telangana
records.description: A monumental statue of Dr. Ambedkar on the Hussain Sagar lakefront in Hyderabad, unveiled on 14 April 2016. It is among the tallest statues in India and is a public monument rather than a museum object.
records.significance: Represents the 'public monument' category of memory, distinct from the house museums and pilgrimage sites elsewhere in the map view.
records.source: Government of Telangana records on the statue.

records.title: Dr. Ambedkar International Centre — New Delhi
records.description: An institution in New Delhi dedicated to research, documentation and public programmes on Dr. Ambedkar's work and on social justice policy, managed under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
records.significance: Functions as the real-world counterpart of this digital archive: a documentation and research institution, and the natural partner for hosting the platform.
keywords: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
records.source: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation.

records.title: 14 October 1956 — Ka Dhamma / the Nagpur conversion
records.description: At Nagpur on 14 October 1956 Ambedkar took the three refuges and the five precepts and embraced Buddhism, together with his wife Savita Ambedkar and a very large number of followers who converted in the same ceremony. He then administered the 22 vows he had framed for the new adherents.
records.significance: The event is observed annually at Nagpur as Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din, and it concludes the Legacy Archive's timeline.
records.source: Standard accounts of the conversion ceremony, October 1956; Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches.

media.label: Visualisation: the Nagpur grounds, 1956
media.note: Procedurally generated. Not an authentic photograph.

records.title: Dr. Savita Ambedkar (1909–2003)
records.description: A medical doctor, married to Dr. Ambedkar on 15 April 1948 and known within the movement as Maisaheb. She looked after his health and studies in his last years, travelled with him to Nagpur in 1956, and after his death worked in the Buddhist and social movements until her death in 2003.
records.significance: Introduced in the Legacy Archive as a physician and a public figure in her own right, with her own documentation rather than as an appendage to the biography.
records.source: Standard biographical record; accounts of the 1956 conversion.

records.title: 6 December 1956 — death in Delhi
records.description: Dr. Ambedkar died in his sleep at his residence at 26 Alipur Road in Delhi on 6 December 1956, a few weeks after the Nagpur conversion and while working on 'The Buddha and His Dhamma'. He was cremated at Dadar in Bombay on 7 December 1956.
records.significance: The date is observed each year at Chaitya Bhoomi and across India. It closes the Legacy Archive's timeline and is handled in a restrained memorial register in the game.
records.source: Standard biographical record; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation.

records.title: Bharat Ratna awarded posthumously — 1990
records.author: Government of India
records.description: Dr. Ambedkar was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, posthumously in 1990. The award was announced by the Government of India and conferred in the same year.
records.significance: The point at which the national recognition recorded in the Legacy Archive begins; followed by the naming of institutions, awards and public programmes after him.
records.source: Government of India award records, 1990.

media.label: Visualisation: citation panel
media.note: Generated panel, not a photograph of the award.

records.title: Dr. Ambedkar Foundation — 1992
records.author: Government of India
records.description: A society established by the Government of India under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to preserve Dr. Ambedkar's legacy through memorials, publications, scholarships and public programmes, including the Dr. Ambedkar National Memorial in Delhi and centres in other cities.
records.significance: The institutional owner of the physical archive that this digital platform is designed to extend — a direct fit with the SIH26096 problem statement.
keywords: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
records.source: Dr. Ambedkar Foundation, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.

records.title: “Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar: Writings and Speeches” — the collected edition
records.location: Government of Maharashtra (compiled and edited by Vasant Moon)
records.author: Government of Maharashtra; Dr. Ambedkar Foundation
records.description: The collected edition of Ambedkar's writings, speeches, papers and letters, published in successive volumes from 1979 by the Government of Maharashtra and later extended by the Dr. Ambedkar Foundation. It is the standard citation source for his texts and is the source used throughout this archive.
records.significance: The bibliography backbone of the whole platform: the archive's citation style is modelled on this edition.

records.title: Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas) — observed since 2015
records.author: Government of India
records.description: 26 November is observed as Constitution Day to mark the adoption of the Constitution in 1949, with reading of the Preamble and civic-education programmes in schools and institutions.
records.significance: The public-programme counterpart of the Constitutional Gallery's content and a natural annual campaign for this platform.
records.source: Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment; Government of India notification, 2015.

records.title: People's Education Society and Siddharth College — 1945–1946
records.author: B. R. Ambedkar (founder)
records.description: Ambedkar founded the People's Education Society in 1945 to open higher education to students who had been excluded from it. Siddharth College of Arts, Science and Commerce in Bombay opened in 1946, followed by Milind College at Aurangabad in 1950 and other institutions.
records.significance: The clearest realisation of the education-first programme of his organisations; the Legacy Archive's education wing is built around it.
records.source: People's Education Society institutional record; standard biographical accounts.

records.title: How this archive is organised — the digital metadata schema
records.author: Platform documentation
records.description: Every record in this archive carries an identifier, title, category, historical period, date, location, author, description, keywords, a citation to a source, and a media list in which each item is marked as either an institutional holding or a generated reconstruction. Records are grouped into six zones, linked to each other through a related-items field, and indexed for the in-game search and for the Archive Guide retrieval layer.
records.significance: This is the record that explains the platform itself: the schema is the deliverable that lets an institution add content without changing any game code.
records.source: Platform documentation — not a historical source.

records.title: Closing note of the Digital Heritage Journey
records.author: Platform documentation
records.description: The final screen of the journey returns the visitor to the argument of the archive: that a constitution is a set of promises and that the record of a life spent making those promises enforceable is held in documents, books, memorials and institutions — which is what this archive exists to keep.
records.significance: The narrative close of the game, followed by the completion certificate and the archive statistics dashboard.
records.source: Platform documentation. The user-facing text is authored, not quoted from a historical source.
